extraction.name: PIQA: Reasoning about Physical Commonsense in Natural Language
extraction.description: A benchmark dataset for physical commonsense reasoning, consisting of multiple-choice question-answer pairs derived from how-to instructions. The dataset tests the ability of natural language understanding models to link text to a robust intuitive-physics model of the world.
extraction.creator: Yonatan Bisk, Rowan Zellers, Ronan Le Bras, Jianfeng Gao, Yejin Choi
extraction.publisher: Association for the Advancement of Artificial Intelligence (AAAI)
extraction.citeAs: Bisk, Y., Zellers, R., Le Bras, R., Gao, J., & Choi, Y. (2020). PIQA: Reasoning about Physical Commonsense in Natural Language. In Proceedings of the AAAI Conference on Artificial Intelligence.
extraction.rai:dataCollection: Data was collected by asking human annotators to provide semantic perturbations or alternative approaches to instructions from instructables.com. Annotators were prompted with links to instructables to inspire them to construct two component tasks: a physical goal and a valid solution, as well as a 'trick' (an invalid but subtly plausible solution). The dataset was cleaned using the AFLite algorithm to remove stylistic artifacts and spurious biases.
extraction.rai:dataManipulationProtocol: The AFLite algorithm was used to perform systematic data bias reduction by discarding instances whose feature representations were collectively highly indicative of the target label. This involved fine-tuning BERT-Large on a subset of data to compute embeddings and using an ensemble of linear classifiers to identify and remove annotation artifacts.
extraction.rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: Data was cleaned of basic artifacts using the AFLite algorithm. Examples with low agreement during validation were removed. Data was tokenized using Spacy and GPT BPE tokenizer. Examples were truncated at 150 tokens. The dataset was split into training, development, and test sets.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: Annotators were asked to glance at instructions from instructables.com and construct a physical goal, a valid solution, and a 'trick' (an invalid solution that sounds reasonable but is wrong due to subtle misunderstandings of preconditions or physics). Annotators were paid an average of >$15/hr. Qualification HITs were used to ensure annotator quality (>80% accuracy on well-formed pairs). Validation HITs were used to remove examples with low agreement.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationPlatform: Amazon Mechanical Turk (implied by 'HIT', 'onturkerview.com', and 'Annotator pay')
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis: During validation, examples with low agreement were removed, often those requiring expert-level knowledge. Annotators used both simple linguistic tricks (negation, numerical changes) and swapped key actions/items for topically similar but unhelpful ones. A diff button was included in the interface to highlight differences between solutions to improve accuracy and speed.
extraction.rai:machineAnnotationTools: AFLite algorithm, BERT-Large, Spacy, GPT BPE tokenizer
extraction.rai:dataSocialImpact: The dataset aims to evaluate and study physical commonsense understanding in natural language models, highlighting the gap between human and machine performance. It seeks to advance research into building language representations that capture details of the real world, potentially aiding robotics and embodied AI.
extraction.rai:dataBiases: The dataset was constructed to be adversarial to BERT and to address reporting bias found in traditional QA tasks. However, it relies on human-generated tricks which may introduce subtle biases in deception. The AFLite algorithm was used to mitigate stylistic artifacts and spurious biases that could artificially inflate model performance.
extraction.rai:dataLimitations: The dataset focuses on everyday situations with a preference for atypical solutions. Some 'mistakes' by models may be correct but require web search to verify. The dataset may not cover all physical phenomena and relies on text-based instructions, which may not fully capture physical interaction. Human performance was calculated by majority vote, and automated methods trained on large web crawls may eventually surpass human performance.
extraction.rai:dataUseCases: Benchmarking progress in physical commonsense understanding, evaluating large-scale pretrained transformer models (GPT, BERT, RoBERTa), and diagnosing the extent of physical knowledge in language models.
